article.title: Most Dangerous Branch
article.author: Sharon Kyle, Dick Price
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Alexander Hamilton famously described the judiciary as the “least dangerous” branch of government. Unlike Congress, it controlled no purse. Unlike the president, it commanded no army. Its principal power was judgment. More than two centuries later, that description is being put to the test. In a special Left Coast Forum discussion presented by LA Progressive, USC law professor Jody Armour joined constitutional scholars Marjorie Cohn and Stephen Rohde to examine a much larger question than whether the current Supreme Court is conservative: Is the Roberts Court fundamentally changing the constitutional balance of power? That distinction matters. Courts have always issued decisions that large portions of the country strongly oppose. But Cohn and Rohde argue that something more consequential is happening today. Across cases involving presidential power, voting rights, independent federal agencies, immigration, guns, campaign finance and reproductive rights, they see a Court steadily transferring power away from Congress, administrative agencies and ordinary citizens—and toward the presidency and the Supreme Court itself. The Rise of the Unitary Executive Cohn began with one of the most consequential ideas underlying the current constitutional struggle: the unitary executive theory. The Constitution divides governmental authority among three branches designed to check one another. But the expansive version of unitary executive theory gives the president extraordinary control over the executive branch, including agencies Congress deliberately attempted to insulate from political pressure. That theory became particularly significant with the Supreme Court's 2024 presidential immunity decision. Cohn emphasized the extraordinary scope of the ruling: presidents receive absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for exercises of their core constitutional authority and presumptive immunity for other official acts. Rohde sees a fundamental contradiction. Conservative justices frequently invoke the intentions of the nation's founders through “originalism.” Yet, he argued, those same justices are enabling precisely the concentration of governmental power that the framers feared. George Washington warned against concentrating legislative, executive and judicial authority in the same hands because such accumulation was the essence of tyranny. For Rohde, the danger becomes particularly acute when one political movement exercises enormous influence over all three branches. When Precedent Becomes Optional The panel also examined the Court's treatment of stare decisis—the principle that courts generally adhere to previous decisions. Precedent is not absolute. Brown v. Board of Education , after all, required the Supreme Court to reject earlier constitutional doctrine supporting racial segregation. But Rohde argued that the Roberts Court increasingly treats precedent not as a stabilizing principle but as an obstacle that can be discarded when it conflicts with the majority's ideological objectives. The most dramatic example is Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization , which overturned Roe v. Wade and eliminated the constitutional right to abortion that Americans had relied upon for nearly half a century. The same conflict is appearing in disputes over independent federal agencies, where the Court has questioned longstanding restrictions on a president's ability to fire officials Congress intended to operate with some political independence. The consequence reaches far beyond individual commissioners. If presidents can remove officials simply because they disagree with their decisions, agencies intended to rely upon professional expertise can increasingly become extensions of presidential political power. Related: Build a United Front against Fascism and a Workers Party Voting Rights and the Courthouse Door Cohn focused particular attention on voting rights. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 was one of the central achievements of the civil rights movement. Yet the Roberts Court has steadily weakened its protections. The problem is not limited to what rights remain on paper. Rohde emphasized another, less familiar doctrine: standing. Before courts decide whether someone's constitutional rights have been violated, plaintiffs must establish that they have the legal right to bring the case at all. A restrictive approach to standing can therefore prevent courts from ever reaching the constitutional question. “The right can be difficult to enforce,” Armour observed, “if the people harmed cannot get through the courthouse door.” That seemingly technical doctrine can have enormous political consequences. Governing Through the Shadow Docket Another transformation receives considerably less public attention: the Supreme Court's growing use of its emergency, or so-called shadow, docket. Traditional Supreme Court cases normally involve extensive briefing, oral argument and written opinions explaining the justices' reasoning. Emergency decisions can happen much differently. Cohn explained that the Court increasingly makes enormously consequential decisions through abbreviated proceedings, sometimes without oral argument and with little explanation. Although these orders may technically be temporary, they determine which government policies remain in effect while litigation proceeds. That means temporary decisions can change people's lives long before the Court ever issues a final opinion. The emergency docket has become particularly important in disputes involving immigration, federal workers, executive authority, election rules and government programs. Related: UCLA 9/11 Symposium Sparks Battle Over Academic Freedom Is the Supreme Court the Most Dangerous Branch? By the end of the discussion, Armour returned to Hamilton's famous characterization. Has the “least dangerous branch” become the most dangerous? Cohn offered an important qualification. The Supreme Court may not itself be the most dangerous branch. Instead, she suggested, it may be enabling the most dangerous branch by removing constitutional restraints on presidential power. Rohde described the presidency and Supreme Court as “the most dangerous twins” in the present constitutional crisis. Their concern ultimately reaches beyond any single Supreme Court decision. It is about whether the constitutional system of separated powers remains capable of restraining government itself. “We the People” Yet the discussion did not end with nine justices. Armour asked what ordinary people can possibly do when Supreme Court justices hold lifetime appointments. Cohn's answer was succinct: organize, litigate, pressure Congress, write letters, protest and participate politically. Rohde went further. “The Constitution begins with the words ‘We the People,’” he reminded the audience. Throughout American history, constitutional change has not come exclusively from courtrooms. Abolition, labor rights, women's suffrage and civil rights required movements outside the courts that eventually transformed what government institutions were willing—or forced—to do. Related: The 2026 Midterms May Not End on Election Day Litigation remains important, Rohde argued, but lawsuits alone cannot protect constitutional democracy. Citizens must understand what the Court is doing, challenge elected officials about judicial appointments and constitutional reform, organize in their communities, demonstrate and vote. That may ultimately be the most important lesson of the conversation. The Constitution is not merely a document interpreted by nine people in Washington. It is a political compact whose survival ultimately depends upon millions of people insisting that its promises—and its limits on governmental power—still matter.
